item.title: Keeping Mathematical Conferences Human
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: As AI makes it increasingly easy to produce polished mathematical papers, slides, and explanations, conferences may have an opportunity to become more interactive and more human. I suggest experimenting with conversational talk formats, where chairs and audiences can ask questions throughout, encouraging discussion, clarification, and a deeper shared understanding of mathematics.
item.content:encoded:
Marco Trombetti, Professor at Università degli Studi di Napoli

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

For a long time, the standard format of a mathematical conference talk has been remarkably stable. A mathematician stands in front of a room. There are slides, or a blackboard. For twenty, thirty, or fifty minutes, the speaker explains a piece of work. At the end, if time remains, there may be a few questions. This format has always had limitations. But I wonder whether the arrival of increasingly capable AI systems gives us a new reason to reconsider it.

In a previous post, I argued that one of the important problems of AI-generated mathematics will be humanization. It is not enough that a mathematical argument exists, or even that it is correct. Someone should understand it, reorganize it, explain why it works, and connect it to the rest of mathematics. Perhaps conferences will have to adapt to the same problem.

A polished talk no longer tells us very much

Suppose I want to talk about a paper at a conference. An AI system may have helped substantially in producing the mathematics. It may have written parts of the argument, reorganized the exposition, prepared the slides, generated examples, suggested explanations, and perhaps even written the script of my talk. In principle, I could give a very polished presentation of a piece of mathematics that I understand only superficially.

Of course, something similar was possible before AI. People have always been able to present work they did not completely understand, and talks have never been examinations of their speakers. But AI changes the scale of the problem. Producing twenty beautiful slides explaining a technical argument is becoming very cheap. Producing a plausible explanation of why a theorem is interesting is becoming cheap. Producing answers to anticipated questions is becoming cheap.

Understanding the mathematics is not necessarily becoming equally cheap.

There is therefore a strange possibility: mathematical communication may become increasingly polished at exactly the same time that the connection between the person communicating the mathematics and the person (or machine) that actually produced the ideas becomes weaker. Perhaps the traditional conference talk is not particularly well designed for this situation.

What if a talk were a conversation?

I have been wondering about a different format. Imagine something closer to an interview than to a lecture. The speaker sits with a chair or moderator in front of the audience. The speaker still presents the work, perhaps with slides or a blackboard, but the presentation is not a forty-minute uninterrupted monologue. Instead, the chair interrupts.

Why did you introduce this definition?

What happens if this hypothesis is removed?

Can you explain the main idea without the technical machinery?

Where exactly does the difficult part of the proof occur?

Is this lemma really necessary?

How did you arrive at this argument?

What is the simplest example in which the phenomenon appears?

The chair would have read at least part of the paper beforehand and prepared a few questions. Members of the audience could also intervene during the discussion rather than waiting for the final three minutes. In spirit, it might look a little more like a late-night interview than a traditional mathematical lecture.

I do not mean that mathematics conferences should become entertainment shows. There need not be a desk, a band, and applause after every theorem. Although I would not completely rule out the band. The important difference would be that the presentation becomes interactive.

Understanding becomes visible

There is something that is quite difficult to fake in a sustained mathematical conversation. If you really understand an argument, you can usually move around inside it.

You can explain it from another direction. You can say which assumptions are essential. You can produce a small example. You can explain what you tried before finding the right proof. You can react when someone asks a question you did not anticipate. You can admit which part you do not understand as well as you would like.

This does not prove that you personally discovered the mathematics. Nor should it. Mathematics is collaborative, and AI will presumably become another participant in that collaboration. I do not think conferences should become detective agencies attempting to determine which sentence was written by a human and which by a machine. The interesting question is different. Has the mathematics passed through a human mind? Can the person presenting it actually discuss it? Can the result enter a mathematical community as something that people understand, rather than merely another object that has been produced?

If the answer is yes, then I care much less about whether AI was involved in obtaining it.

There would be some pressure

There is an obvious objection. This format would be more stressful. Standing in front of an audience is already stressful enough for many people. Being interrupted by a senior mathematician asking questions could make things considerably worse. I do not think this objection should be dismissed.

In particular, younger researchers should not be placed in a situation where a conference talk becomes a public oral examination. The same is true for mathematicians who are not comfortable speaking English, people who are naturally less quick in conversation, or anyone for whom this kind of interaction creates a substantial disadvantage. Understanding mathematics and performing well under pressure are not the same ability.

Any new format would have to recognize this. Perhaps junior researchers could receive some or all of the questions in advance. Perhaps the chair could meet the speaker before the session and discuss the structure of the conversation. Perhaps traditional talks could remain available for people who prefer them. Perhaps questions could be deliberately explanatory rather than adversarial. The point should not be to catch the speaker making a mistake. The point should be to create a setting in which understanding naturally becomes part of the presentation.

But perhaps a little pressure is useful

At the same time, I am not sure that all pressure is bad. If I know that presenting a paper means that someone may ask me why Lemma 4.7 is true, I have a rather strong incentive to understand Lemma 4.7 before I submit the paper. If I know that I may have to explain why a certain definition is natural, I may spend some time thinking about whether I actually know why it is natural. And if an AI system has generated an argument that I do not understand, perhaps I will be less tempted to immediately turn it into a conference submission if I know that eventually I will have to sit in front of other mathematicians and discuss it.

This seems healthy. At present, AI dramatically reduces the cost of producing mathematical text. Perhaps our institutions should increase the reward for understanding that text.

The chair would have a new role

This would also change the role of the session chair. At many conferences, chairing a session currently consists mainly of introducing the speaker, watching the clock, and saying “perhaps one last question.” In a conversational format, the chair would have a genuine intellectual role. The chair might read the paper beforehand, identify its central ideas, and prepare questions that help the audience understand what matters. A good chair could rescue a difficult presentation by asking exactly the question that half the room wants to ask but does not know how to formulate.

This work would take time, of course. But perhaps it should. We spend enormous amounts of collective time attending conferences. It seems slightly strange that so little time is usually invested in designing the actual intellectual interaction that happens there.

It might make conferences better anyway

There is another possibility. Perhaps this would be a better conference format even if AI did not exist. Many mathematical talks are extremely difficult to follow. A speaker has fifty slides and forty-five minutes, the notation accumulates, one crucial definition is missed, and twenty minutes later a significant fraction of the audience has become spectators rather than participants. A chair who can interrupt and say, “Before we continue, could you explain again what this object is supposed to represent?” might improve the talk enormously.

Questions during the presentation could reveal which ideas actually interest people. The speaker might spend less time covering every theorem in the paper and more time explaining the one idea that people will remember six months later. We might discover that the purpose of a conference was never really to reproduce the contents of papers orally. Papers are quite good at containing the contents of papers. A conference should perhaps do something else.

It should create understanding, discussion, disagreement, connections, and memories.

Conferences as part of verification

I have argued elsewhere that AI-generated mathematics may require new mechanisms of verification and humanization. Perhaps conferences could become part of that process too. Not formal verification. Not peer review. Not an examination establishing authorship. Something softer.

A result arrives in the mathematical community, and someone has to stand behind it, or perhaps better, sit beside it, and talk about it with other mathematicians. The audience sees not only a theorem and a proof, but a human being navigating the ideas around them.

Questions expose unclear points. Experts notice connections. Someone asks about a missing case. Another person suggests a simpler argument. The speaker realizes that one explanation is much better than the one in the paper.

The talk becomes another stage through which mathematical output is transformed into shared mathematical understanding.

An experiment

I certainly do not think every conference should replace all talks with interviews next year. Perhaps the format would fail completely. Maybe the speakers would hate it, or the chairs would not prepare enough. Perhaps discussions would constantly run over time. Perhaps the best researchers would turn out to be terrible interviewers and the best interviewees would not necessarily be the best mathematicians. These are good reasons to experiment rather than legislate.

A conference could try one session. Five speakers. Twenty or thirty minutes each. A chair who has received the papers beforehand. Ten minutes of presentation mixed with questions and discussion. Questions from the audience throughout. For junior participants, the questions could be discussed in advance. Then ask everyone whether they learned more.

My suspicion is that we eventually need to rethink several mathematical institutions that were built for a world in which producing mathematical text was expensive. Journals are one of them. Authorship is another. Conferences may be another.

If machines can increasingly produce papers, proofs, slides, summaries, and polished explanations, then perhaps the scarce object is no longer mathematical text. Perhaps the scarce object is understanding. And if that is true, our conferences should be designed to make understanding visible.

item.title: Slow Maths
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: For a long time, I had the ideal job. As a teacher, I passed on not just mathematics, but also the taste for critical thinking, for confrontation, and the joy of discovery.
item.content:encoded:
Isabelle Gallagher, head of the French Mathematical Society

For a long time, I had the ideal job. As a teacher, I passed on not just mathematics, but also the taste for critical thinking, for confrontation, and the joy of discovery. As a researcher, I contributed my small part to the greater endeavour, alongside the wider mathematical community. I was part of this collective adventure, which I believed would never end. Slowly, insidiously, however, some flaws began to appear. We elevated colleagues to the status of heroes and heroines for their technical prowess and for the number of their publications in so called prestigious journals. We awarded an ever-increasing number of prizes, with ever-larger sums, to a small number of individuals, organisations or institutions, often focusing more on their productivity and reputation than on the substance of their work, or its inherently collective nature. We watched, amused or even flattered, as a Foundation placed a prize in dollars on a small list of mathematical problems to be solved within the millennium. And we used international competition and the lack of institutional funds as excuses to embark on a frantic race for publication, without taking the time to reflect on the fundamental purpose of our work. Over the past few months, doping has become a major issue in our profession. You can obtain it by yourself, or sometimes the institution provides unlimited access to it. At first, it was simply a matter of asking ChatGPT to check a bibliography, rephrase a paragraph, proofread a calculation or improve it. Then it became possible to ask directly to perform the calculation, or even to work out the correct calculation to perform. Now we can act as ‘super-prompters’, putting hundreds or thousands of agents to work to explore as many avenues as possible, having them correct each other’s work, letting them come up with ideas, and thus ‘crack’ one after the other doctoral subjects, problems that colleagues are working on, or those that the Clay Foundation has considered to be the most important. The ecological cost of this new way of practicing
mathematics is not addressed. What price is the mathematical community prepared to make humanity pay to answer its questions? Soon, the AI industries will have grown tired of testing and refining their models on our questions, using our very work we make available to them. In the meantime, we will have turned our profession into an ultra-doped race. In the face of this transformation, it is both urgent and essential that we return to the original purpose of our work and rethink the way we assess it. I dream of a new way of practicing mathematics, one that does not require us to resort to ‘doping’ just to stay in the race. It would be ‘slow maths’, just as there is ‘slow food’ or ‘slow tourism’. A form of maths where we have a firm control of its structure and objectives. Maths that allows us to stray down side paths which sometimes turn out to be more beautiful and more interesting than the one we originally set out to explore. Maths where we take the time to reflect, to write, to explain, and to share. This practice of ‘slow-math’ is essential because it is not the final result that matters and enables us to go further, but rather the process itself, the detours, and the collective endeavour. I am convinced that it is ‘slow-math’ that will help society progress collectively and soundly, and enable young people to continue wanting to learn, to question and to understand. This practice is now only possible if we collectively decide to put an end to the race to publish, and if we agree to value the idea that can lead to a result just as much as the techniques that finalize the proof, and just as much as proofreading, rewriting, and the sharing of ideas and methods. Only then will we be able to leave the race behind, take the time to understand things in depth, and once again practice the ideal profession.

item.content:encoded:
Dora Woodruff, Hanna Mularczyk and Anna Brandenberger, graduate students at MIT

In late September and early October, we (three graduate students from MIT) conducted a survey of early career mathematicians. Our goal was to give grad students and postdocs a centralized, targeted platform to share their views on AI. The personal stakes are highest for grad students and postdocs, who face job insecurity and funding instability. We worry that our concerns will be deprioritized, or even misrepresented, without collective resources like this survey.

On October 29th, we posted the results of this survey to the arXiv (history and overview). In the end, over 260 mathematicians, representing around 60 institutions and 5 countries, filled the survey out. Many of them left long, thoughtful free responses in addition to answering the multiple choice questions.

This post is an invitation to take a look at the survey results. Some questions surprised and/or dismayed us: in particular, Question 3.2, Question 3.3, and Question 5.2. It’s also important to point out that nearly all of the responses were collected before October 6th: we nervously wonder how different this data would look today. As journals, hiring committees, and faculty members make decisions about the community’s future, we urge you to take these survey results into account — and keep proactively talking with the junior researchers in your orbits.

[ArXiv Link]

AI was not used to write/edit the post or the arXiv article.

item.title: Please STOP writing papers! (there is another way)
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: The number of papers submitted to the mathematics sections of arXiv is exploding, recently prompting arXiv to impose a cap on submissions per author. As an editor, I also see a substantial rise in submissions to mathematics journals. This is very worrying: the current publication system cannot absorb such a volume of papers. […]
item.content:encoded:
Mathieu Lewin, CNRS and University Paris Dauphine PSL

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

AI statement: I wrote the initial draft and revised it with ChatGPT’s assistance to polish the English and improve clarity. ChatGPT was also used to screen the arXiv submissions automatically.

The number of papers submitted to the mathematics sections of arXiv is exploding, recently prompting arXiv to impose a cap on submissions per author. As an editor, I also see a substantial rise in submissions to mathematics journals. This is very worrying: the current publication system cannot absorb such a volume of papers. Many will have to remain unpublished. Some journals have even temporarily stopped accepting new submissions.

I took a closer look at arXiv’s “Analysis of PDEs” section (math.AP). The number of papers in this section has increased by a factor of 2.45 in one year: from September 15 to October 14, there were 1,302 papers in 2026, compared with 531 over the same period in 2025. That is 771 additional papers in PDE alone.

Much of this increase is likely due to AI, even indirectly (some authors may be rushing to finish their old-fashioned “brain-crafted” papers before AI supersedes their results). An automated screening of the 1,302 PDE papers found that 493 explicitly disclosed using AI. Most of these, however, reported using it only for language editing and proofreading, which alone cannot explain such a sharp increase. Only 173 papers (13.3%) explicitly reported using AI to generate or develop parts of their proofs.

This is going nowhere. We should use these new AI tools to do new things, rather than ten times more of what we were already doing before AI.

In this post, I will argue that much of the problem comes from our obsession with writing papers, even when another form of publication would be more appropriate. I will propose a new type of technical report, which I will call an “AI proof report.” Establishing guidelines for these AI proof reports is one of our community’s most urgent tasks if we are to prevent our publication system from collapsing. Finally, I will discuss what I believe belongs on arXiv and in mathematics journals.

The obsession with papers

This obsession is already built into the AI models themselves, probably reflecting the fact that we mathematicians do not know what else to do. ChatGPT and Claude tend to present their answers as mathematical papers, complete with a title and abstract, using the amsart LaTeX document class, even when we have not asked for this.

This tendency reached an unprecedented level when OpenAI posted more than 700 “papers” on GitHub on October 6. All were dressed up as mathematical articles, but none could seriously qualify as one in its present form. Even those that resolve an important conjecture would require substantial further work before publication in a mathematics journal. The proofs are largely unreadable. The introductions are generally poor and overlook important contributions to the subject. The choice of references is puzzling. Too little technical detail is provided about how the proofs were produced.

I am deeply concerned to see some of our colleagues also turning to the industrial-scale production of AI-generated papers. I will refrain from naming names, but many readers will recognize the pattern. These colleagues pick whatever conjectures they can find, even outside their own areas of expertise, and race to solve them first, as though playing a video game. Once they obtain a proof, they upload a paper to arXiv, submit it to a leading journal, and move on to the next conjecture. They do not take the time to make the proofs readable, perhaps because they do not understand the arguments themselves.

These AI-generated proofs may have considerable scientific value. For the sake of discussion, let us assume that they are correct (although establishing this for the most complicated arguments may require formalization and verification in a proof assistant such as Lean). Correctness alone, however, does not make an argument a mathematical paper. We still need to turn it into something we can understand and reuse in other contexts. Until that work has been done, these outputs should not be dressed up as papers. Instead, we should treat them for what they are: valuable raw data that require further scientific analysis.

AI-generated proofs as raw data

I have read many blog posts and essays about AI in mathematics, including on this website, and I am surprised by how rarely contributors draw comparisons with other fields. We occupy a small corner of science, both in numbers and in funding (in France, mathematics accounts for only about 3% of public research). I cannot help wondering what other scientists think of our current situation.

Mathematics is unusual in how little its day-to-day practice has changed over the past century. By contrast, most other scientific disciplines rely on experiments, often using sophisticated and expensive equipment. Obtaining good experimental data requires considerable expertise. The data must be carefully collected and organized according to established protocols. Only then can scientists analyze them and draw conclusions.

There are well-established standards for producing, presenting, and sharing data. Data should be structured, clearly labeled, and stored in an open, nonproprietary format. A data report should include enough technical and descriptive metadata to allow others to interpret and reuse the data.

I believe we should take a similar approach to AI-generated proofs. An AI proof report should briefly describe the context and history of the problem, without necessarily providing the full introduction expected of a research article. It should state which parts have been checked and how, identify any known gaps, and provide access to the code, formal proofs, or other supporting files needed to examine the argument. It should explain how the proofs were produced, specifying the model and prompts used and, in the case of a multi-agent system, the number of AI agents, their respective roles, and how they interacted. It should also make the structure of the proof clear. For long arguments, a map showing the logical dependencies between intermediate statements could be useful. The report should make the role of AI explicit, rather than presenting the generated arguments as the authors’ own work. We could develop a dedicated LaTeX class for these AI proof reports and require AI models to use it. Such AI proof reports could also contain supporting computations for a research article.

These AI proof reports should be collected in a community-owned repository where everyone can read, comment on, revise, and reuse the material. They should not be posted to arXiv or submitted to mathematics journals. They can serve as starting points for further research or as supporting material for a paper, without having to take the form of a journal article.

Throughout this discussion, I am treating arXiv as a preprint server for papers intended for journal publication. With that role in mind, we need a separate repository for AI proof reports. The recently launched website hexagonmath.org seems to reflect some of the concerns outlined above and could serve this purpose. For now, however, it accepts “research works of all kinds,” and clear guidelines for presenting AI-generated proofs seem to be missing.

What belongs in journals and on arXiv

Our research papers are already far more technical and less accessible than those in other scientific disciplines. Very few people read the technical parts of a mathematics paper in detail. We should not let AI make this situation worse. We could even use this opportunity to make our papers more accessible.

I strongly believe that research articles should be written primarily for human readers, who should be able to follow the argument from beginning to end. Giving readers greater priority is what will save our publication system.

Experimental sciences offer a useful model: because the full data cannot be included in an article, authors must select and explain the evidence needed to support their conclusions. When the LIGO and Virgo collaborations announced the first direct observation of gravitational waves, they did not reproduce all the data in the paper. Instead, they made the relevant data available through a dedicated website, with documentation and a DOI. Readers could thus examine and analyze the data underlying the published results without those data having to appear in the article itself.

We should take the same approach to AI-generated proofs. Unless they are short and simple, or have been fully rewritten and explained in a way that human readers can follow, they should not appear in our papers. Initially, they might be included as supplementary material. But I expect that they will soon become so long and difficult to read that storing them separately and citing the relevant AI proof report will make more sense.

Like other forms of raw data, AI-generated proofs require careful scientific analysis before they can lead to a research article that humans can fully understand. This takes time and effort. We value simple, general arguments because we can understand and remember them. These are the insights we should try to extract from an AI-generated proof and ultimately present in a mathematical paper.

Extracting an idea does not necessarily mean reading an AI-generated proof line by line, which may be impractical for the longest arguments. And we should certainly not offload the task of checking these arguments line by line onto PhD students or postdocs! In fact, experts may be better placed to spot a promising idea because they know the background and previous attempts. I do not yet know how best to gain insight from a complicated AI-generated proof, such as those OpenAI recently dumped on the mathematical community. We may need help from the AI models themselves in this process. What I do know is that the papers emerging from this material will need to be very different from the texts produced by the models.

I am deliberately leaving open what counts as “human-readable.” It certainly means more than a proof that can, in principle, be checked line by line. Many proofs written by humans are not particularly readable either! As always, referees and editors will have to judge whether the exposition is sufficiently clear. None of OpenAI’s 700 “papers” would pass that test in its present form.

In the future, some steps in our proofs may still require computer assistance, with their correctness certified by Lean or another proof assistant. There is no shame in this: computer-assisted proofs already have a long history, from Appel and Haken’s proof of the four-color theorem in 1976 to Hales and Ferguson’s proof of the Kepler conjecture, announced in 1998. Some areas of mathematics require extensive computations. Wherever possible, these should be confined to a few clearly identified steps, with the code and details of their verification provided separately.

The lengthy and demanding work of analyzing an AI-generated proof need not be carried out by those who produced it. Producing the material and extracting mathematical insight from it can be separate contributions. Anyone can use prompts to generate potential proofs, including people who pursue mathematics as a hobby: this is a form of citizen science. Recognizing a genuinely new and useful idea in the output, however, requires expertise. We may need to form working groups and undertake this analysis more collectively than before, which could be a welcome development.

Even after we have digested an AI-generated proof, rewritten it, or developed something entirely different from it, it may still be worth preserving the original output in an AI proof report. This would make our own contribution clearer and give others the opportunity to draw different insights from the same material.

Final recommendations

Whether we like it or not, AI is already part of mathematical research and is likely to remain so. Many mathematicians already use it daily. My message in this post has two parts. First, we should give greater priority to readability in research articles. I am not sure that banning AI from research papers would solve the problem, since we cannot reliably verify authors’ declarations of how they used it. As editors and referees, we should instead apply a familiar principle more firmly than before: recommend for publication papers that we like and think other human readers will like too. Papers that are original, well written, and likely to have a substantial scientific impact. Papers whose arguments we can follow and understand. The difficulty and technical complexity of a proof should no longer be the main criterion.

Second, we should recognize the potential scientific value of AI-generated proofs, even in their raw form, before the work of analysis and interpretation has been done. We should encourage those who produce them to share their findings as AI proof reports in an appropriate repository, following common guidelines. These reports should be recognized as valuable contributions in their own right, with proper credit given to their authors.

So, if you have obtained an AI-generated proof of an important conjecture but are not prepared to do the hard work needed to turn it into a paper that others can understand, please do not dress it up as one. Share it first as an AI proof report, rather than posting it to arXiv or submitting it to a mathematics journal. Unreadable proofs are likely to be rejected. Establishing that a theorem is true is no longer enough to justify a research article. Deposit the report in an appropriate repository. Then contact experts on the problem and let them know what you have found. They may suggest revising parts of the argument or testing other approaches. Your report can receive a DOI and be credited to you. Good data can attract many citations, bring you recognition, and make a valuable contribution to mathematical knowledge.

item.title: What Does AI Do for Olympiad Students?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “There's a solid argument that AI has solved the IMO, in terms of being able to output LaTeX that would score a 7 on most or all of the questions, virtually guaranteeing highest honors there and at similar contests. Despite this, what I've seen within the community is that AI has not meaningfully affected contests or preparation for them. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Beckett Bradford, high school student in New York City, taking college classes at NYU

There’s a solid argument that AI has solved the IMO, in terms of being able to output LaTeX that would score a 7 on most or all of the questions, virtually guaranteeing highest honors there and at similar contests. Despite this, what I’ve seen within the community is that AI has not meaningfully affected contests or preparation for them. AI has definitely changed how many students study, and has, for example, proved Erdős #41, though only after prompting by a former gold medalist. Yet it hasn’t caused a crisis in contest integrity or massively enhanced students’ abilities.

This is not to say AI is having no effect on competitions. At Canada’s take-home test, the Repêchage, a potential route to their IMO team, the cutoff for advancement was a perfect score for the first time in the test’s history, prompting its discontinuation because of cheating concerns. At proctored tests, though, student performance has thus far been more or less unaffected.

I’ve heard some people dismiss AI solving contest problems as not a meaningful capability, since those problems are explicitly designed to be solved with techniques a competition-inclined high schooler would know, rather than the vast corpus available to people designing AI systems. I disagree with this. AI’s ability to solve these problems is notable and can be useful, even if such abilities, from my own experience, translate poorly to being able to write good olympiad problems. Not all old problems have readily available solutions, and many students use these tools as a search substitute if they’re stuck, or researching a topic.

AI solutions often use unanticipated, sometimes circuitous, approaches. Occasionally they write very good ones. In my own experience, I came up with a problem I found interesting and was able to solve it in about forty minutes with a rough write-up. Afterward, I gave the problem to GPT-6, and it found a much cleaner solution with a different approach in about three minutes.

AI’s lack of impact on learning beyond writing solutions and fixing grammar is, I think, an interesting divergence from the human, since many fantastic contests are organized and run by former olympiad students. For the past few years there’s been noise about how AI will “revolutionize” learning by giving everyone an on-demand personal tutor that adjusts to them, designing personalized tests, and so on. Khan Academy launched its own effort towards this with an experimental chatbot2, with the ambition that it would “prompt critical thinking.” Now, after three years of advancements in AI, usage remains low. And the major labs have mostly abandoned their respective study modes.

AI has, thus far, not been a step change from regular search engines. Notably, Google has shied away from continuing to pour hundreds of billions of dollars into frontier intelligence, while still pursuing less ambitious AI products.

Thankfully, most students and peers I talk to aren’t excessively concerned about the future of human math’s relevance. They are happily trying to complete their projects, study a new textbook, and share their enjoyment of the field.

A privilege of studying mathematics is its unusual openness. At the competition level, we practice old olympiads from the Netherlands to Indonesia. In the past month I’ve spoken to people from Hong Kong, Italy, Brazil and more, about various bits of problem solving. Interestingly, US AI labs withhold their products from Hong Kong.

By and large, I feel the effects of AI on non-technical tasks are negative, from the prevalence of slop images to the cavalcade of vibe-coded websites. Removing friction mostly invites users who have either momentary interest or are compelled by “AI UNLOCKS INFINITE MONEY!!! CLICK HERE!!!” AI has recharged perennial memes from “college is dead” to “this is the final generation that will experience scarcity.” I notice a lot of this is reminiscent of early internet excitement, with claims like “Google has made college irrelevant” and “we are now at the beginnings of a global civilization, a new civilization of civilizations, that will blossom through the coming century.” I’m sure some people thought the same when their local public library opened. AI does not seem to be a step change so much as it is one of efficiently routing existing knowledge, often leaving its origin obscured.

The costs of AI use and investment, particularly in the USA, have also been rising. At time of writing, the latest publicly available OpenAI model saturated a major evaluation at a cost of roughly twenty-six thousand dollars3, and these labs will need to move their revenue at least one order of magnitude to keep pace with projections over the next two years.

From my perspective, with, I admit, limited experience in higher math, but a good deal in problem solving and exposure to people involved in higher math, I don’t think math is in crisis, or, I hope, that pure math majors will not face significantly worse prospects than five years ago.

Along with near-unlimited funding and laissez-faire regulation, the AI companies behave recklessly and have created large amounts of public distrust, with the explicit goal of making “intelligence” a utility akin to energy. Where between inept investor relations and a truly held belief in the cyber eschaton this originates from isn’t relevant here. Most notable to math, of course, has been the Navier-Stokes controversy, which I won’t comment on beyond saying that the USA AI labs’ view of research principally as an investor slide has made many influential people who were enthusiastic about AI’s potential uses weary of the labs’ idea of “cooperation.”

The labs, perhaps noticing a bad news cycle, have been quick to move on to bigger things like armageddon. Unfortunately, the drumbeat of doom, and calls for government intervention, are succeeding in convincing some people to fear a rogue AI apocalypse. Anxieties about the future are constant and wide-ranging, from awards cutoffs and college admissions to climate change. Yet concern that discovery itself will soon be automated by USA companies is the most directly commercial I’ve heard.

Despite the companies’ behavior, I remain optimistic about AI’s overall use as an assistive tool. I’ve personally found it great at turning sketches into clean TikZ diagrams. And I’ve seen sincerely interested people use AI in creative ways, leveraging it to improve their own work. The best AI is now probably better than any individual at olympiad problems, but this is a narrow piece of olympiad math. Broadly speaking, AI can’t be a community of ambitious students or create good handouts. We can only know if its solutions are relevant if we solve the questions ourselves.

Below are two articles skeptical of AI’s economic future I think are worth reading:

  • Warning Signs (New Left Review, Sidecar)
  • AI Bubble Monitor (CEPR)

item.title: Collaborative work groups on exposition problems
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Fear of being scooped leads to unpolished preprints intended to claim priority. Could such undesirable flag-planting behavior also arise for expository work on key results? Starting from this premise, this post proposes that collaborative working groups offer a healthier way forward.
item.content:encoded:
Alexander Van Werde, Postdoctoral Researcher at Mathematics Münster, Germany

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

A significant worry in our community is a potential widening gap between human understanding and formal problem solutions. This issue has been increasingly apparent due to AI systems’ ability to generate long formally verified proofs. A common sentiment is that it would help if we assigned more credit to exposition.

A related issue is the pressure that authors experience to put an unpolished preprint online to avoid being scooped. Sometimes, this unpolished state may only be temporary. However, the expertise needed to polish the writeup is not always present for AI-generated results. The expertise required for a first proof was reduced by AI systems, but it is likely still needed for digestion and exposition.

Could the rush that leads to unpolished preprints arise for exposition too? If an author gets recognized for an acceptable writeup, then others may get less credit for better exposition. For well-known problems, it is plausible that multiple people are working independently. This makes accidental scooping more likely, so authors might be incentivized to rush.

One approach is for authors to announce that they are working on it. However, this encourages the exact flag-planting behavior that initial unpolished preprints are associated with. Moreover, others may also want to digest the ideas, and collaboration could be beneficial!

I propose that it may be better to announce collaborative work groups:

  1. Someone in the field, who may not be the original author, forms a group intended to work on the exposition and digestion of a preprint. This group announces its existence. Further, the group states what additional expertise it would benefit from.
  2. The group creates a blog or Git repository where it openly reports on partial progress. For instance, an initial report could discuss the previous literature, addressing a common problem in AI-generated manuscripts. Subsequent reports could release expositions on parts of the technical content, as the digestion proceeds.

    Such reports would be valuable to the community. The ideas used to resolve a central problem may also be relevant elsewhere, so having some quick updates would be useful. Further, this would make it clear that the group is not merely a flag-planting operation.

The end goal could be to produce a human-written manuscript with good exposition that can be submitted at classical venues. This would allow the hard work of exposition to be acknowledged within the incentive structures that currently exist.

The reasons why such groups could be particularly suitable for expository work are as follows:

  1. A single author asserting ownership feels silly when the solution was generated by an autonomous AI system. The solution then properly belongs to the community. An open collaborative approach would hence be more natural, while still rewarding the people that worked on the exposition with demonstrable research output.
  2. The engagement of a group of people would help to disseminate the ideas. This group would naturally be trained to pursue and appreciate follow-up activities, such as searching for generalizations or applications of the tools in different problems.
  3. While a proof can in principle be generated and formally verified in an arbitrarily short time span, human digestion has natural limits. Hence, the latter activity particularly requires a slower process. This would be aided by the protection from accidental scooping that follows from the announcement of the group’s existence.

Such groups do not need to be huge. Having too many collaborators incurs communication difficulties and can lead to “design by committee” where the exposition lacks a unified vision. However, the idea is that the term “collaborative work group” would signal an open attitude, where collaborators are welcome subject to reasonable constraints. Initial arXiv announcements of unpolished preprints often feel like an author marking their territory, the exact opposite signal.

I am curious what others think. It appears that a central repository with such work group announcements could be useful. There could however also be downsides. For example, the act of engaging with improperly written preprints might appear to legitimize their production.

item.title: A new system of accreditation
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: I propose the following: the main way that a mathematician obtains "credit" for new results should be by writing publications which are at the level of doctoral theses and defending them in front of the mathematical community. The community can then give this publicly available reviews. Hiring committees then look at someone's list of such publications, taking into account the community's comments to judge quality if they so desire, and make hiring decisions based on that.
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Ng, PhD student at the University of Bonn

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

It has become clear in recent years, and especially after the advent of LLMs, that the current publication system of journals is untenable and inequitable. I think this is an excellent opportunity to reform the system, so let me outline a suggestion.

I propose the following: the main way that a mathematician obtains “credit” for new results should be by writing publications which are at the level of doctoral theses and defending them in front of the mathematical community. The community can then give this publicly available reviews. Hiring committees then look at someone’s list of such publications, taking into account the community’s comments to judge quality if they so desire, and make hiring decisions based on that.

Concretely, how this would work is the following. Every year, everybody who has defended a PhD thesis has the right to ask for a defence of one of their preprints. (PhD theses are defended the same way as before.)

These are not submitted to any journals; we abolish journals by agreeing that nothing which is received from the 1st of January 2029 will be refereed or quick opinioned or given any of the unpaid and unacknowledged labour that journals need to function. In place of journals, some sort of international organisation, such as the IMU, receives requests from mathematicians to defend a preprint, which is uploaded to said organisation’s website and/or the arXiv. For simplicity’s sake let’s pretend that the IMU does this so I don’t have to write international organisation, but I want to emphasise that it need not be the IMU or any existing organisation: it could be a new thing entirely. The IMU then appoints someone to examine the publication, akin to how examiners examine doctoral theses. Theses should be tagged with keywords/ MSC codes etc, and all mathematicians who have defended a thesis or publication in related areas have the right to rate this by writing comments on a system hosted by the IMU’s server. These are publicly available and must be tied to the reviewing mathematician somehow. For instance, one might have to use ORCID to access this system, but the ORCID would not be publicly available (probably only to the examiner, if at all). The criteria used could be elegance of the argument, novelty of the techniques, and depth, as measured by establishing connections to other problems which are not obviously related or connections to other areas of mathematics.1

After a period of at least 3 months (also subject to debate, but some time so that there is enough time for others to read the publication and for the author incorporate comments, corrections etc.), a defence of the preprint should take place, broadcast online so that other people may take part. The purpose of this is for the author to convince the community of the correctness and interest of the results in the preprint, and to explain the proof/methods to all those who are interested. I cannot stress the importance of the latter enough: it is imperative that we cure ourselves of Hardy’s disease2. All present should additionally rate the defence on quality of exposition. At the end of the defence, the examiner should compile the opinions of the mathematicians who have rated the preprint, decide whether the defence was successful, and write a longer report. If successful, the preprint is published along with the examiner’s report and all the opinions of others who have rated them. The quality of a publication is judged by the examiner’s report and the collective opinion of the mathematicians who have rated it, but there are no more or less prestigious “places” to defend since all defences are centrally administered. This sort of publication is what is considered in the “proving results” part of hiring/promotion decisions.

Why do this, and how do other existing practices change/adapt?

This may sound like a lot of work. That’s because it is. However, I believe that in the age of generative LLMs a publication should merit this amount of work in order to be deserving of publication. As we all know by now, just having a proof of some theorem is not indicative of anything. It should form part of some larger body of work that points to new directions in research, and that is what, allegedly, a doctoral thesis is meant to be.

Since this is a lot of work for the examiner in particular, I believe that in career-related decisions, committees should weight examining a publication as highly as defending one. Examiners should be given credit for their work regardless of acceptance. Since the examiner is supposed to understand the publication well, responsibility for explanation and exposition of the results in the publication should fall on both the author and the examiner.

I think this proposal has a reasonable claim to stopping the arms race in publishing papers. I have heard senior people lament that students are now pressured to publish papers earlier and earlier, and that has the effect that often students don’t think about things as deeply as they used to. The proposed system incentivises everybody, not just PhD students, to think deeply about whatever mathematics they are engaged in. To prevent people from just shoving random results together and calling that a preprint, I suggest that we give the examiners the right to say that the results of a preprint are incoherent and there is no unifying theme. I would also say that preprints can be defended jointly if most of the results were obtained in collaboration, but the preprint should count towards the quota of all the authors.

I believe that a defence where one can grill the speaker is much better for communicating understanding/expositional purposes. I agree with Frank Calegari here that “the median mathematics seminar could (perhaps harshly) be described as a waste of time for both the participants and the speaker”. In talks where I am actually interested in the speaker’s results, I have found the introductory spiel to be uninspiring, and to take up too much time so that the new results are only very cursorily alluded to. I cannot press the speaker on the details of their methods, because this could be considered heckling, derail the conference schedule, and disturb their flow. Consequently, I get nothing out of the talk and have to resort to pestering the speaker afterwards. I think if we really wanted to get anything more than a superficial acquaintance with the speaker’s work out of a talk, that talk has to resemble a doctoral defence more than it does a conference talk in the current model.

What of the arXiv? I think this is a great endeavour and we should work to preserve it. I think people should continue uploading preprints to the arXiv, and that the authors of a preprint have the right to use the results in it in a defence and call those “their results” for the next two years3 after uploading. This is so that people can stake claims to results and not get scooped while they work on building their narrative. After the two year period, the results should be considered as folklore4: they can be used by anyone in a defence. The purpose of having an expiry date at all is this: some people choose not to fully explain or clean up their arguments, sometimes never publishing them. This results in an undesirable situation: obviously someone should do this work so that it can be verified, digested, and incorporated into the community’s repertoire, but there is currently no incentive to do this, since it would be, generally speaking, unacknowledged labour. Having an expiry date rewards someone who is willing to put in the effort to understand the mathematics in an orphaned preprint and integrate it into the community. This also deals with the issue of AI company produced preprints. Let’s take the construction of a complex structure on S6S^6 as an example. Engel took the initial 100 page preprint and turned it into a much more readable 20 page preprint (although I tried to read it, it is still beyond me since I don’t have the background in complex geometry, but I am told it is much better). In my proposed system, the result is his to claim, and I think this is fair.

While we are on the topic of reforming the system, I would also like to propose that the IMU have a dedicated branch towards public outreach and exposition, and substantial contributions towards this goal should be weighted the same as contributions such as defending or examining publications. Converting mathematics into something that the general public can appreciate is very hard work which deserves to be recognised. The public has funded our research and they deserve to get something out of it as well. If we do not want to rely on the blood money of the finance and tech companies and be beholden to their whims, we must convince the public that what we do is of value to them5. I admit that I do not know how best to do this, but there are many people who have experience with successfully engaging with the public, and that expertise should be tapped.

I have dreamt up this system based on the assumption that it is depth of understanding that we want to preserve and encourage. I would like to address the concern that this is somehow unfair to the people who prefer problem solving, and I will say what I mean using combinatorics as an example. I think that it is fine to enjoy problem solving. I do. But I think that when doing research, especially in this day and age, just solving the problem isn’t enough. One should find better and/or alternative ways of solving the problem6, and try to hit on methods/techniques/heuristics which apply more generally. For instance, Turan’s theorem has a number of different proofs, many of which generalise to other problems or hint at more general theory which can be explored. If, in a hypothetical universe which had adopted this system, somebody had discovered what we call Turan’s theorem, then what they could do next is solve more Turan like problems and publish a treatise on forbidden subgraphs. Similarly, Erdos’ introduction of the probabilistic method to bound Ramsey numbers is an ingenious and extremely elegant argument, and one which is taught to many undergraduates for good reason: it generalises. If someone had discovered the probabilistic method, they could then prove some number of other results that were previously inaccessible and then write a publication on this method and how great and good it is. I have been taught, and have taught others, that solving problems helps you solve more problems. Research papers should show this in action.

LLMs

I have thus far been a bit coy about the exact status of LLMs in mathematics in this proposed universe. Only time will tell, but from my perspective the current unregulated system poses an existential risk comparable to that of nuclear weapons, if not worse. In my opinion, private companies absolutely should not be allowed to train any sort of large language model or AI. I agree with others who believe that such LLMs, trained on so much public data, should also be a public good whose benefits the public should reap7. If we do believe that LLMs should continue to exist and play an important role, then they should be set up in such a way that it is accessible to as large a proportion of the public as we can manage, run on sustainable energy, and not have data centres popping up left right and centre. Mathematicians would then have access to this (open source) LLM. Perhaps access to LLMs/tokens/queries could be allocated in a similar way computing time on supercomputer clusters is. I have added this partly because, at a Maths and AI panel in Bonn, a panelist asks whether we would be willing to accept access to a slightly weaker model than what the AI companies have, and someone responded it depends on how we are assessed as junior mathematicians. I believe that the proposed system mitigates, to some extent, the inevitable difference between levels of AI access across different institutions.

There is also the massive uncertainty of what LLMs will be capable of in the future. They will, with high probability, be able to formalise arguments without much difficulty, so I have not paid much attention to verifying the formal correctness of preprints. I assume this will be dealt with as the times change.

There is still the issue of whether LLMs could generate publications at the level of doctoral theses that seem to be as good as human ones and have viewpoints which we find aesthetically agreeable. It would be foolish to bet against this, and I do not know how to get around this (yet), but I find Tarik Aougab statement from a previous post appealing: ” By definition, AI cannot be better than humans in the activity of human beings talking to one another. So insofar as humans sharing ideas with other humans is an essential part of what it means for mathematics to exist, this question is actually beside the point. In fact, there is nothing automatically wrong or bad about a human using an AI to help themselves understand some piece of mathematics in order to then go and explain it in a new or interesting way to another human or group of humans. But this is only doable at all if human mathematicians learn to value– and even reward – conversation.”.

I have a bit more to say about this sort of question/objection. First of all, I believe that, as Uri Bader said in an earlier post, maths just exists. The Poincare conjecture and Fermat’s Last Theorem have always both been true, but the point of research in these directions was to uncover why they are true, what structure lies beneath, and how they are connected to a great many other, often unexpected, questions in mathematics. And then communicate all of this to other people so that they might further build on that and learn even more about the mathematical universe. The Book of God has been written since the dawn of time and just because someone/something else can read it doesn’t that any individual or community has to stop trying to read it.

Second of all, suppose that tomorrow some alien race came to Earth and said that they are technologically much more advanced so we puny Earthlings should cede control over all our institutions, stop all research and scientific endeavours, and just do what they tell us. If this happened in a film and the people collectively shrugged their shoulders and said ok, I think most viewers would rightly call those people idiots. Now that this is happening in real life8, I don’t think it is wise or prudent of us to leave our fates in the hands of people or technology of dubious9 trustworthiness.

Training students

On the topic of training students, I think very little has to change if we adopt these community norms. We can still teach and test for understanding, creativity, quality of exposition, choice of direction/questions, perseverance etc. All of the things which the system claimed to teach before the advent of LLMs. Perhaps some amount of work would have to go into thinking about how best to integrate LLMs into one’s workflow, but that is a relatively minor issue.

I would also like to address the oft-repeated analogy with chess, as somebody who, in a past life, spent a lot of time playing and studying chess. As other commentators have pointed out, chess is fundamentally different to maths: it is a finite game, played as a competition between two players. Maths is not finite, as far as I can tell, and it is not a competition in my view: it is a search for the truth. When chess engines arrived, this changed the game in the sense that the best player is no longer a human being, but it is still as enjoyable as it was before, and competitions are still between human players. The existence of extremely powerful LLMs impacts the field of maths differently, of course, but for illuminating which parts of the infinite search space we, as humans, find interesting, it seems to me that humans should be the ones to decide.

The most important lesson to be learned from chess, however, is when it comes to training students. The reader may already know this, but chess players have never ever improved by just reading what the chess engines spit out. Coaches always tell students to think about positions without an engine first, and only after a fair amount of thought maybe turn on the engine to see what they have missed. For all intents and purposes, the most powerful chess engines are oracles, and there are correct ways to use them to improve. I believe the same applies to mathematical oracles too, and it is up to the individual mathematician to figure out what the correct way is10, but we cannot possibly hope to do so in the current journal system which has such perversely distorted incentives.

2. Criticisms, Drawbacks, Alternatives

I admit that this proposal is far from perfect. For instance, there is still a fair amount of subjectivity and bias in this system, but I don’t see how we could eliminate that completely if we insist on a large human aspect of the profession. I don’t know if we want to argue that we can/should eliminate subjectivity completely. This proposal is very much inspired by thinking about how academia in other disciplines works: in computer science papers are defended at conferences, but they also have the problem of slop, so one must raise the bar somehow, and I have opted for something similar to the practice of writing books that is commonplace in the humanities.

In earlier conversations about a version of this proposal I was told that I was insanely optimistic and had never experienced a system where widespread corruption was the norm11. This is because I suggested that there should additionally be numerical ratings for the judging criteria, and that the person attached to ratings/comments should be public. There are good reasons for having anonymous refereeing: to prevent “you scratch my back, I scratch yours” kind of behaviour, and because people might feel uncomfortable giving their peers honest negative feedback if their name is attached to it12. It is still possible that it is worth having numerical ratings which are only available to the examiner, but many people have pointed out to me the drawbacks of having explicit numerical ratings that are public, such as these being one-dimensional metrics which committees will use instead of considering mathematicians holistically, or this devolving into a social media-esque popularity contest.

As for choosing the examiners, in this industry it is usually an open secret who is corrupt or who doesn’t get along, so this can be avoided when choosing examiners, who I believe really should be publicly known. This is of course very much up for debate, but I think that journals deciding what to publish based on the opinions of a couple of arbitrarily chosen referees and a handful of overworked editors who often aren’t that related to the area of the submitted manuscript is insane and fertile ground for corruption. There is also the concern that this puts too much burden on the ‘senior’ people. I would imagine that the examiner doesn’t have to be the most senior person in the field: anybody who is competent and objective would do perfectly well, just as postdocs referee papers currently.

I have gotten multiple questions on the issue of how to assess the standards of examiners’ work. I think this has to be because their identity and the report that they write are public. The argument that anonymous refereeing is objective is, in my opinion, dubious since it offers no way of ensuring that the referee did their job properly. I also expect that no person will be allocated the task of examining more than once or twice a year, so there shouldn’t be any incentive to do a bad job to collect more ‘examining credits’.

I was asked an interesting question that I had not thought of: if I insist that every publication be at the level/scope of a doctoral thesis, what happens to small/cute results that don’t manage to get used/fit into some narrative? My suggestion is that they simply get left as preprints on the arXiv. It seems to me impossible to award very many credits for a small thing which might end up really being a prompt and not very many tokens away in the age of powerful generative LLMs. Perhaps they could get published in a sort of maths magazine like EMS press, or one could send them to a maths contest (e.g. Miklos–Schweitzer), or if enough of these are accumulated one could publish them as a book. Alternatively, one could obtain two types of credit: big theses level credits which are what is taken into consideration in career decisions, and smaller community level credits for this sort of thing.

This question in turn arose because, in an earlier draft, I considered the possibility of everyone having the right to 3 defences a year. I’d argue that very few people can consistently write 3 doctoral theses a year, but this probably does not alleviate the pressure to publish. This lead me to the suggestion of everyone having the right to a single defence every year, which I got from Lawk Mineh, where they report on what they have done since their last defence (but are not obliged to defend every year). This potentially lets the small/cute results in. However, if there are too many small results that are spread across too wide an area, it makes it difficult for any single examiner to assess the publication as a whole. I’m sure there are refinements/ways around this, but I do favour more directed efforts to tell a story about a part of mathematics rather than just a smattering of very loosely related results.

3. Conclusion

I do think that most versions of what I have suggested are strictly better than the current unsustainable journal system13, and absent any better suggestions this system is something that we should move towards. It has also been pointed out to me there is no need to try to enforce this very much, since it is aligned with the interests of the community and the institutions that fund us. I was told that CNRS spent a whopping 3 million euros on publishing fees in 2025, and not a single cent of this went to anybody who did any mathematical work. I think that, upon reflection, mathematicians will collectively realise just how ridiculous the publishing system is and how little it actually serves the interests of the community. It would be best if the proposal were to get tested, and given the new journals for video recordings of talks, I hope it’s not too much of a stretch for some slightly more senior people to give a proposal like this a test run and see what works, what doesn’t, what needs tweaking, whether it is workable etc.14 Let me also offer something so that it doesn’t seem like I am just telling others what to do15. If there is consensus around a proposal for what defences should look like and people would want to test it to see how that works, I am willing to test that out on my defence in summer 2027. If it comes to it, every single mathematician in the world is welcome to come and grill me about my thesis.

  2. From G. H. Hardy’s A Mathematician’s Apology: “There is no scorn more profound, or on the whole more justifiable, than that of the men who make for the men who explain. Exposition, criticism, appreciation, is work for second-rate minds.” I can think of no single sentence in the history of mankind that has done more harm to mathematics. ︎

I like this very much in principle, but I am concerned that this does not sufficiently incentivise pushing the boundaries of knowledge. For instance, I would probably spend too much time learning other people’s results, since I enjoy this, but at some point someone ought to produce something new. ︎

item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: The mathematical literature contains mistakes. Articles on the arXiv are not refereed, and even peer review does not guarantee that articles are error-free. Tim Gehrunger, Postdoc at ETH Zurich

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

The mathematical literature contains mistakes. Articles on the arXiv are not refereed, and even peer review does not guarantee that articles are error-free. In private communication, many (tenured and non-tenured) colleagues have told me that they now run their drafts through an AI model before posting, and that this sometimes catches serious mistakes. The capabilities of AI to catch mistakes seem to have improved drastically in the last months.

In a recent study for MathArena, we asked GPT-6.1 Sol to extract the main theorems of arXiv papers and search for explicit counterexamples to these theorems. Each counterexample was then verified and classified by severity. Across 656 papers from January 2025 to July 2026, the model reported major errors in about 6% of papers. For 137 papers from August and September 2026, a period in which over a quarter of arXiv papers began acknowledging AI use, that rate fell to 1.5%.

A likely explanation is that some authors already ran an AI check and fixed what it found. Part of the effect may also be because more recent work is partly AI-generated, and a model may have a harder time finding errors in an AI-generated argument. Still, the trend matches what people are telling me and my personal experience.

Our suggestion is to do an AI check before posting a manuscript, and there is evidence that many mathematicians are already doing so. Also, it is very likely good practice to run your older papers through an AI check to see if any results need fixing.

Full write-up and data: J. Dekoninck, T. Gehrunger, K. Rögnvaldsson, C. Sun, M. Vechev, Searching for errors in mathematical papers with GPT-6.1 Sol, MathArena, October 2026. https://matharena.ai/literature_mistakes/
